1.pericope_label: The LORD made a covenant with us in Horeb: I stood between

schools.summary: Give the grammatical warrant for reading the denial as comparative: this is the usage of the Hebrew language in drawing contrasts, so the sense is not only with our fathers, who actually heard it, but with us also, who were in the loins of our fathers, and for whom the covenant was intended no less than for them. Add the arithmetic, that every man above forty-two at the time of this discourse might actually remember the day at Sinai. But if the denial is taken as a real exclusion, say who is excluded and name those you reject: the fathers are neither those who died in the wilderness, as Augustine supposed, nor the forefathers in Egypt, as Calvin imagined, but the patriarchs. On face to face, be exact about the Hebrew, since the phrase used here is not the one used of God speaking to Moses; that expresses the very confidential relation in which the Lord spoke to him as one friend to another, whereas this denotes simply the directness with which Jehovah spoke to the people, that he came as near to them as one person to another. And note that though he talked with them face to face they saw no manner of similitude and no visible form: the very words of God reached their ears, and nothing more.

Read the denial as not with them only, on the authority of the Jewish commentators, since the law was certainly given to the immediate fathers of this generation, whose carcasses had fallen in the wilderness; unless the more remote ancestors are meant, with whom the covenant of grace was made, the law not being delivered until four hundred and thirty years later. On face to face, deny the familiar sense: it does not mean the free, friendly and familiar manner in which God talked with Moses, but that he spoke publicly, audibly, clearly and distinctly, without the interposition of another and without making use of anyone to relate what he said. And commend the law by the certainty the people had of it, for when God openly manifested himself there could be no doubt of the author from whom it proceeded; he set before their eyes a visible manifestation of his glory by appearing in the fire, since no other voice but his own could proceed out of fire. Then reconcile the two things that seem to contradict, that God spoke in person and yet by a mediator, since the people, having heard his voice, petitioned in their fear that he would not continue to speak in the same way.

Settle the third verse by supplying two words: the Lord made not this covenant with our fathers only, but with us also. Then take the first verse as a ladder of five steps, since the order is the point: God speaks to the people; the people are called to hear what God speaks; to learn what they heard, that they may be thoroughly instructed in the will of God; to keep his testimonies ever in mind, treasuring them in a believing and upright heart; and to do them, obeying the whole will of God and taking his word for the invariable rule of their conduct. Then ask the question the ladder invites: should not all these points be kept in view by every Christian assembly? On the fourth verse, take face to face as personal and immediate, not by the mouth or ministry of Moses, plainly and certainly, as when two men talk face to face, and freely and familiarly, so as not to overwhelm and confound them.

Begin with the summons and the attention it demands: hear and heed, hear and remember, hear that you may learn and keep and do, else your hearing is to no purpose — for the end of hearing and learning is not to fill our heads with notions or our mouths with talk, but to rectify and direct our affections and conversations. Then see the wonderful condescension of divine grace in turning the command into a covenant, that we might be the more strongly bound to obedience by our own consent and the more encouraged by the divine promise; it is the promises and threatenings annexed to some of the precepts that make them amount to a covenant. On the parties, hold that it was not made with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, to whom God gave the covenant of circumcision but not that of the ten commandments, the light of divine revelation shining gradually so that the children were made to know more of God's mind than their fathers had. And take the mediator standing at the foot of the mount as a type of Christ, who stands between God and man to show us the word of the Lord, a blessed days-man that has laid his hand upon us both, so that we may hear from God and speak to him without trembling.

debates.question: Is the denial 'not with our fathers' absolute or comparative?

sides.position: Comparative, by the Hebrew usage in drawing contrasts: not only with our fathers, but with us also
A real exclusion — and the fathers excluded are the patriarchs, not those who died in the wilderness nor the forefathers in Egypt

debates.question: Does 'face to face' imply the familiarity of friends?

sides.position: Yes: it is equivalent to discoursing openly and familiarly, God speaking with them as mortals and friends communicate
No: the Hebrew phrase is not the one used of Moses, which expresses a confidential relation; this denotes only the directness of the address

outliers.note: Alone settles the identity of 'the fathers' by naming and rejecting two earlier answers, that of Augustine, who took them for those who died in the wilderness, and that of Calvin, who took them for the forefathers in Egypt.
Alone converts the grammatical point into a fact about the audience, calculating that every man above forty-two at the time of this discourse might actually remember the day at Sinai.

Alone turns the opening verse into a graded sequence of five duties, from God's speaking to the people's doing, and closes by asking whether all these points should not be kept in view by every Christian assembly.

themes: And Moses called all Israel, and said unto them, Hear, O Israel, the statutes and judgments which I speak in your ears this day, that ye may learn them, and keep, and do them.
The Lord our God made a covenant with us in Horeb.
The Lord made not this covenant with our fathers, but with us, even us, who are all of us here alive this day.
The Lord talked with you face to face in the mount out of the midst of the fire,
(I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to shew you the word of the Lord: for ye were afraid by reason of the fire, and went not up into the mount;) saying,

6.pericope_label: From the first commandment to the keeping of the sabbath day

schools.summary: Take the first commandment word by word. Before me is literally upon my face, in addition to my presence, or as one Jewish commentator has it, in any place where I am, which is the whole world — idols being at best only masks which man puts upon the face of God, insulting to his dignity and tending to conceal him from view. Settle the visiting of iniquity in two sentences rather than a disquisition: it is not meant that the soul of the son shall die for the father, the penalty extending only to them that hate God; and no sins so surely entail consequences on later generations as the abominations of idolatry. Then read the two clauses together, for as love here is practical, so is hatred in the verse before: to hate God is to disobey his commandments.

Spend the strength of the comment closing an escape route. Idolaters endeavour in vain to elude the prohibition by distinguishing two kinds of honour, reserving the higher for God and paying the lesser to pictures and statues; but Moses first comprehends all the forms and ceremonies of worship and then adds the word which properly means to serve, so the evasion is childish. And even granting the distinction they do not escape, since the prohibition amounts to God's declaring that he will not be worshipped in wood and stone or any other likeness; for unbelievers were never carried so far into folly as to adore mere statues, having always alleged something behind them. On the visiting of iniquity, state the difficulty at its full strength — that nothing is more unreasonable than that the innocent and the guilty should be involved in the same punishment, and that the prophet's declaration is well known, that the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father but the soul that sinneth shall die — and then answer that the prophet was refuting a false complaint, since not one of those with whom God was severe was free from crime, and that God is at liberty to punish the crimes of the fathers upon their descendants, with the proviso that these too may be justly punished as imitators. On the promise, refuse to read it as a debt: God does not say he will be faithful or just towards the keepers of his law but merciful, and grace is not promised severally to every descendant of the saints, since there were many degenerate children of Abraham. Rest the argument on the disproportion — vengeance limited to the third or fourth generation, mercy extended to a thousand — which shows that he plainly prefers to attract men by gentle invitations rather than extort obedience by terrifying threatenings. Alongside this, note more briefly that the commands are delivered in the same order and nearly the same words as before.

Turn the commandment into examination, and put the questions to the reader rather than answer them for him: have you worshipped God in spirit and in truth, proposed no end besides him, sought no other happiness than the knowledge and love of God, and found in him the desire of your eyes and the joy of your heart? If not, thou hast other gods before him.

Account for the repetition before expounding anything: though these words had been spoken before and written, they are again rehearsed, for precept must be upon precept and line upon line, and all little enough to keep the word of God in our minds. Then face the variation from the earlier record honestly rather than deny it, and draw the rule it teaches by comparing the two forms in which the Lord's prayer has come down to us: we must tie ourselves to the things rather than to the words unalterably, since the sense is what binds and not the syllables.

debates.question: Is this rehearsal of the commandments verbally the same as the first giving of them?

sides.position: There is some variation, and the variation itself teaches that we must tie ourselves to the things rather than to the words unalterably
They are delivered in the same order and nearly the same words

debates.question: How does visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children escape the charge of punishing the innocent?

sides.position: By the fathers' guilt and the children's imitation: none with whom God was severe was free from crime, and he may punish the crimes of the fathers upon descendants who are justly punishable as imitators
By the limiting clause itself: the penalty extends only to them that hate God, and idolatry above all sins entails consequences on later generations

outliers.note: Alone anticipates and dismantles the defence of image-worship that distinguishes two kinds of honour, arguing that Moses first comprehends all the forms and ceremonies of worship and then adds the word which properly means to serve.
Alone gives a figure for what an idol is, calling idols masks which man puts upon the face of God, insulting to his dignity and tending to conceal him from view.
Alone declines exposition altogether and converts the first commandment into a series of questions the reader is to answer about his own worship and happiness.

themes: I am the Lord thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage.
Thou shalt have none other gods before me.
Thou shalt not make thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the waters beneath the earth:

Thou shalt not bow down thyself unto them, nor serve them: for I the Lord thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me,
And shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me and keep my commandments.
Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain: for the Lord will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.
Keep the sabbath day to sanctify it, as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee.

14.pericope_label: From the sabbath rest to the tenth commandment

schools.summary: Keep to what the words themselves show. On the fifth commandment note that it is in this longer form, with that it may go well with thee, that the apostle cites it. On the tenth, note that where the earlier text employs one verb this employs two, the idea of the one being to delight in and of the other to lust after.

Notice the copulatives, that these commands begin with the copulative and, differently from the earlier place, which joins them together and to what precedes; hence the law is by some said to be one copulative. On the fifth commandment say plainly that it is the first commandment with promise, the promise being of long life and happiness in the land. On the tenth, take lust to be the thing intended by the words.

Do not choose between the reasons annexed to the sabbath but count them, finding three grand ends in the appointment: to commemorate the creation; to give a due proportion of rest to man and beast, since in Egypt they had none, so that having shown them mercy God teaches them to show it to their servants; and to afford spiritual advantages, keeping the soul in remembrance of the rest which remains. Explain the smaller variation too, that the sabbath day stands here where the earlier text has the seventh, by a change of the day at the exodus, from Sunday to Saturday, effected upon the gathering of the manna — so that the sabbath became a twofold memorial, which accounts for the new reason assigned. Then, observing that little had been said about the spiritual sense of the ten commandments where they were first given, add questions here which the reader may answer between God and his own soul, and run them through commandment by commandment. On honouring parents ask whether he has slighted their advice, supplied their wants, concealed their infirmities, and whether servants have done all things as unto Christ, not with eye-service but in singleness of heart. On the sixth press the commandment far past killing: has he tempted any one to what might shorten his life, or suffered intemperance under his roof; is he guilty of no degree of self-murder, and does he never eat or drink anything merely because he likes it when he believes it prejudicial to his health; and has he not hated his neighbour in his heart, since if he failed to reprove him that sinned in his sight, he has in God's account hated him.

Work by comparison with the earlier record, and explain every difference you find. The reason annexed to the fourth commandment is taken there from the creation of the world and here from the deliverance out of Egypt, and the change is significant: that deliverance was typical of our redemption by Jesus Christ, in remembrance of which the Christian sabbath was to be observed. Observe next that the last five commandments are coupled together here, which they are not in the earlier place — neither shalt thou commit adultery, neither shalt thou steal — and take this to intimate that God's commands are all of a piece, the same authority that obliges us to one obliging us to another, so that we must not be partial in the law, for he that offends in one point is guilty of all. On the fifth commandment mark the added words that it may go well with thee, which the apostle quotes and puts first; and meet the difficulty they raise, that some have been dutiful to their parents and yet have not lived long, by reconciling it thus: whether they live long or not, it shall go well with them, in this world or a better.

debates.question: Why is the reason annexed to the fourth commandment changed from the creation to the deliverance out of Egypt?

sides.position: Because that deliverance was typical of our redemption by Jesus Christ, in remembrance of which the Christian sabbath was to be observed
Because the day itself was changed at the exodus, making the sabbath a twofold memorial; the appointment has three grand ends and the creation remains one of them

debates.question: What is promised in 'that it may go well with thee'?

sides.position: Long life and happiness in the land — it is the first commandment with promise
Something that survives the cases where the dutiful do not live long: whether they live long or not, it shall go well with them, in this world or a better

outliers.note: Alone explains why the text reads the sabbath day where the earlier record has the seventh, by a change of the day at the exodus from Sunday to Saturday, effected upon the gathering of the manna.

Alone leaves exposition for examination, adding questions commandment by commandment which the reader may answer between God and his own soul, and pressing the sixth commandment out to intemperance, self-murder and hatred in the heart.
Alone weighs the two verbs of the tenth commandment against the single verb of the earlier text, distinguishing the idea of delighting in from that of lusting after.

themes: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thine ox, nor thine ass, nor any of thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates; that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou.

And remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the Lord thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the Lord thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day.
Honour thy father and thy mother, as the Lord thy God hath commanded thee; that thy days may be prolonged, and that it may go well with thee, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee.
Thou shalt not kill.
Neither shalt thou commit adultery.
Neither shalt thou steal.
Neither shalt thou bear false witness against thy neighbour.

Neither shalt thou desire thy neighbour’s wife, neither shalt thou covet thy neighbour’s house, his field, or his manservant, or his maidservant, his ox, or his ass, or any thing that is thy neighbour’s.

22.pericope_label: Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God

schools.summary: Take God's adding no more as a statement of sufficiency: a perfect rule of life is contained in the ten commandments, so that when their instruction is fully received the whole body of wisdom is attained and the people need seek no more — when God made an end of speaking, he himself laid down the bounds of legitimate inquiry. Then read the people's own words closely. When they confess that they saw the glory and the greatness of God they oblige themselves to obedience unless they choose avowedly to make war against him; and when they add that God doth talk with man and he liveth they are expressing astonishment at what was scarcely to be believed, since a long period had elapsed since such revelations ceased and they are amazed as at a new thing. Notice then that the two following verses seem to contradict each other, for having found that those to whom God manifests himself are not always destroyed, why should they say they shall die if he continues to speak? Answer that they fear for the future the danger they had escaped by a marvellous indulgence: it is as if they had said that it is more than enough once to have provoked God against us, and of his inestimable loving-kindness that he has thus far pardoned us, so that we must beware lest our perversity bring heavier punishment. Turn the request for a mediator against a temptation nearer home: since the experience of God's ancient people ought to persuade us that when he sets teachers over us he makes the best provision for our salvation, his majesty being intolerable to us if he thundered from heaven himself, this should repress the destructive itching of those who desire God daily to descend, or at least to send his revelations by angels, and who on that account despise the ministry they have. Alongside this, divide the people's two words more simply on one Jewish commentator's authority: the glory means the appearance of fire in which the Lord was, the greatness the thunders and lightnings and the voice of the trumpet.

Read he added no more not as sufficiency but as a change of mode: God ceased for that time to speak immediately and with that loud voice, the rest being delivered to Moses and communicated by him; and this he did to show the preeminence of that law above the rest, and its everlasting obligation. State the purpose of the terror just as plainly: it was a dispensation designed to make the gospel of grace the more welcome, and to be a specimen of the terrors of the judgment day.

Take the same sense of he added no more and turn it into a prohibition: other laws were sent by Moses, but no more were spoken in that manner, and since he added no more we must not add, for the law of the Lord is perfect. Then list what may be inferred from the people's request: that they expected further commands and were willing to hear more; that they thought Moses able to bear discoveries of the divine glory under which they knew themselves unable to stand; and that they were for the moment in a good mind under strong convictions of what they had heard. Add two cautions to the inference. They believed Moses a favourite of Heaven and one who would be faithful to them, yet at other times they murmured at him and a little before this were ready to stone him — see how men's convictions correct their passions. And many have their consciences startled by the law who have them not purified, fair promises being extorted from them but no good principles fixed and rooted.

debates.question: What is meant by God's adding no more?

sides.position: Sufficiency: a perfect rule of life is contained in the ten commandments, and God himself laid down the bounds of legitimate inquiry when he made an end of speaking
Sufficiency, taken as a prohibition: other laws were sent by Moses, but since he added no more we must not add, for the law of the Lord is perfect
Not sufficiency but a change of mode: God ceased for that time to speak immediately and with that loud voice, the rest being delivered through Moses

debates.question: What is the people's request for a mediator chiefly evidence of?

sides.position: Their momentary good frame under strong convictions — and of the limits of it, since many have their consciences startled by the law who have them not purified
God's provision in setting teachers over us, which rebukes those who desire him daily to descend and on that account despise the ministry they have
A dispensation designed to make the gospel of grace the more welcome, and a specimen of the terrors of the judgment day

outliers.note: Alone raises the apparent contradiction between the people's confession that God doth talk with man and he liveth and their fear that they shall die if he speaks again, resolving it as a fear for the future of a danger already escaped by a marvellous indulgence.
Alone sets the people's confidence in Moses against their conduct elsewhere, noting that they murmured at him at other times and a little before this were ready to stone him.

Alone divides the people's two words on a Jewish commentator's authority, referring the glory to the appearance of fire in which the Lord was and the greatness to the thunders and lightnings and the voice of the trumpet.

themes: These words the Lord spake unto all your assembly in the mount out of the midst of the fire, of the cloud, and of the thick darkness, with a great voice: and he added no more. And he wrote them in two tables of stone, and delivered them unto me.
And it came to pass, when ye heard the voice out of the midst of the darkness, (for the mountain did burn with fire,) that ye came near unto me, even all the heads of your tribes, and your elders;

And ye said, Behold, the Lord our God hath shewed us his glory and his greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the midst of the fire: we have seen this day that God doth talk with man, and he liveth.
Now therefore why should we die? for this great fire will consume us: if we hear the voice of the Lord our God any more, then we shall die.
For who is there of all flesh, that hath heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?
Go thou near, and hear all that the Lord our God shall say: and speak thou unto us all that the Lord our God shall speak unto thee; and we will hear it, and do it.

28.pericope_label: O that there were such an heart in them

schools.summary: Deny exactly that reading, and name the abuse: this and similar passages have been ignorantly abused by some to establish man's free will, as if the will were capable of bending either way and man had the power of doing right while God without interfering looked on at the event. Give instead a figurative account of the wish: God assumes a human feeling here, since it would be vain and absurd for him to desire what it is in his power to confer, having the power of bending men's hearts wherever he pleases; speaking in the character of a man, he shows that the people's perseverance was rather to be wished than hoped. Rest the whole on the distinction between the two wills: we must consider God's will as it is set before us in his word, not as it is hidden in himself, for while by his word he invites all promiscuously to life, he quickens by his secret inspiration only those whom he has elected. Give the reason for the wish as well, which the others take for granted — that they would not be so firm and faithful in keeping their promises as they were ready and willing to make them, so that hypocrisy was not altogether banished or purged from their minds; and although the people's answer is to be approved, there will be too much difficulty in the performance for the event to accord with it. Alongside this, settle the question by the grammar instead: there are not properly such volitions and wishes in God, but Scripture speaks after the language of the children of men, and the words may be rendered who will give that they had such an heart — not to me, but to them. From which draw the practical conclusion, that they cannot give such a heart to themselves, nor can any creature give it, and none but God can; therefore they ought to have prayed to him for a heart to hearken and do.

Read the wish as decisive for liberty, and say so in those terms. They refuse to receive such a heart from God, and who then can supply it? If they had not been perfectly free agents, able either to use or abuse their liberty, could God have made the complaint or expressed the earnest desire we find in this verse? He made the human will free, and in spite of all the influence of sin and Satan he preserves its liberty; for had man no free will he could neither be punished nor rewarded, being a mere machine, and no more accountable for his actions than the fire for its consuming quality or the stone for its gravity — the one having burned the house of the righteous, the other having crushed the innocent to death.

Stay out of the dispute and read the wish as evidence of what God is like: the God of heaven is truly and earnestly desirous of the welfare and salvation of poor sinners, and has given abundant proof of it — giving us time and space to repent, inviting us by his mercies, sending his Son to redeem us, publishing a general offer of pardon, and swearing that he has no pleasure in the ruin of sinners. Then turn the wish on the reader, taking it of a heart such as they had at that moment rather than such as they ought to have: it would be well with many if there were always such a heart in them as there seems to be sometimes, under conviction of sin, or the rebukes of Providence, or when they come to look death in the face.

debates.question: Does 'O that there were such an heart in them' establish free will?

sides.position: Yes — God could not make the complaint or express the desire unless they were perfectly free agents; without free will man is a mere machine, no more accountable than fire or a falling stone

No — the passage has been ignorantly abused to that end; God figuratively assumes a human feeling, and his revealed will inviting all must be distinguished from the secret inspiration by which he quickens the elect
No — there are not properly such volitions and wishes in God; Scripture speaks after the language of the children of men, and the words may be rendered who will give that they had such an heart

debates.question: What does the wish show about God's disposition toward the people?

sides.position: That he is truly and earnestly desirous of the welfare and salvation of poor sinners, as his time given to repent, his mercies, his Son and his general offer of pardon all prove
That their perseverance was rather to be wished than hoped, hypocrisy not being altogether purged from their minds and the performance being harder than the promise

outliers.note: Alone turns the grammatical rendering into a duty, arguing that since neither they nor any creature can give such a heart and none but God can, they ought to have prayed to him for a heart to hearken and do.

Alone takes the wish of a heart such as the people had at that moment rather than such as they ought to have, observing that it would be well with many if there were always such a heart in them as there seems to be under conviction of sin, the rebukes of Providence, or when they come to look death in the face.
Alone answers the objection with mechanical images, that a man without free will would be no more accountable than the fire for its consuming quality or the stone for its gravity.

themes: And the Lord heard the voice of your words, when ye spake unto me; and the Lord said unto me, I have heard the voice of the words of this people, which they have spoken unto thee: they have well said all that they have spoken.
O that there were such an heart in them, that they would fear me, and keep all my commandments always, that it might be well with them, and with their children for ever!
Go say to them, Get you into your tents again.

But as for thee, stand thou here by me, and I will speak unto thee all the commandments, and the statutes, and the judgments, which thou shalt teach them, that they may do them in the land which I give them to possess it.
Ye shall observe to do therefore as the Lord your God hath commanded you: ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left.
Ye shall walk in all the ways which the Lord your God hath commanded you, that ye may live, and that it may be well with you, and that ye may prolong your days in the land which ye shall possess.
